items.prompt: What do the letters in the ADDIE instructional design model stand for?

options.label: Aim, Draft, Deploy, Improve, Evaluate
Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate
Assess, Deliver, Design, Interact, Educate
Analyze, Deliver, Develop, Instruct, Evaluate

rubric: ADDIE is Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate.
Distractors mix plausible education words that are not the model's phases.

items.prompt: Which statement best defines a learning objective?

options.label: A list of the topics and readings the instructor will cover
A statement of what learners will be able to do afterward
A summary of what the instructor plans to do in each session
A description of the course schedule, length and assessments

rubric: An objective states the intended learner performance after instruction.
Distractors confuse objectives with topic lists, logistics or materials.

items.prompt: Which verb is best for writing a measurable learning objective?

options.label: Be aware of
Appreciate
Understand
Calculate

rubric: 'Calculate' describes observable behaviour that can be assessed.
Other verbs describe internal states that cannot be directly observed.

items.prompt: In Bloom's revised taxonomy, which is the lowest level of thinking?

options.label: Understand
Apply
Remember
Analyse

rubric: Remember (recalling facts) is the base level.
Understand is the next level and is often mistaken for the lowest.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a needs analysis at the start of a design project?

options.label: To measure what learners retained after the course ends
To find the gap between current and desired performance
To decide which delivery tools and media to purchase
To write the assessment questions for the final test

rubric: Needs analysis identifies the performance gap training should close.
Distractors name tasks that belong to other phases or to non-design work.

items.prompt: Which are parts of a well-formed ABCD learning objective? Select all that apply.

options.label: Audience: the learners who will perform the behavior
Degree: the standard of acceptable performance
Delivery: the medium used to teach the content, such as video or classroom
Condition: the circumstances under which it is performed

rubric: ABCD covers Audience, Behavior, Condition and Degree.
Budget is a project constraint, not an element of an objective.

items.prompt: A designer has finished building a course and its materials. The course is now being rolled out to the first group of employees, who begin their sessions this week. Which ADDIE phase is the team in?

options.label: Design
Implement
Develop
Evaluate

rubric: Delivering the finished course to learners is the Implement phase.
Develop is the phase just completed, which is the common confusion.

items.prompt: Why do designers write learning objectives before choosing activities and assessments?

options.label: Objectives are required by law for every course
Objectives make the course longer and more detailed
Objectives show what activities and tests must support
Objectives let the instructor skip evaluating the results

rubric: Objectives guide the selection of activities and assessments.
Distractors give reasons unrelated to alignment.

items.prompt: An objective reads: 'Learners will list the five ADDIE phases.' At which Bloom level is it written?

options.label: Create
Remember
Analyse
Apply

rubric: Listing facts is recall, which is the Remember level.
Higher levels require using, breaking down or building something.

items.prompt: A short quiz given midway through a course so learners and instructor can see what to fix is an example of which kind of assessment?

options.label: Formative assessment
Summative assessment
Placement assessment
Certification assessment

rubric: Checks during learning that guide improvement are formative.
Summative assessment judges final achievement, a frequent mix-up.

items.prompt: Why is a lecture-only session a weak fit for the objective 'Learners will perform a spreadsheet lookup'?

options.label: Lectures are hard to record, so learners can't review the steps later
Lectures suit knowledge-based objectives better than any procedural one
Lectures give learners too little content to cover the lookup steps
Learners need hands-on practice to build the skill itself

rubric: Activities should match the behaviour in the objective; skills need practice.
Distractors rely on overgeneralised claims about lectures.

items.prompt: The objective is 'Learners will write a professional email.' Which assessments align with it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Drafting an email reviewed against set criteria
Writing an email scored with a rubric
A multiple-choice quiz on the history of email
A vocabulary test defining the word 'tone'

rubric: Aligned assessments have learners perform the stated behaviour.
The other two test recall of related facts, not writing.

items.prompt: Which best explains why designers analyse the learners' prior knowledge?

options.label: It replaces the need to evaluate the course later
It makes the final test easier for every learner
It tells them how much existing skill to build on
It lets them avoid writing any learning objectives

rubric: Prior knowledge determines the starting point and pacing of content.
Distractors suggest it removes other design steps.

items.prompt: A company's trainees score well on a written test of safety definitions, yet many still make errors when operating the machine. The course objective was 'Operate the machine safely.' What best explains the mismatch?

options.label: The test covered too little of the safety vocabulary taught
The test measured recall, not the operating behaviour
The trainees memorised answers without having read the manual
The machine is too complex to be taught through any training

rubric: The assessment was not aligned with the performance objective.
Other options blame learners or the task, ignoring the test design.

items.prompt: Which learning objective is written so that it can be measured?

options.label: Appreciate why the five steps of the returns process matter to customers
Understand how each of the five steps of the returns process works
List the five steps of the returns process in order
Become familiar with the five steps of the returns process in order

rubric: It uses an observable verb, so a learner's success can be checked directly.
Understand, appreciate and become familiar describe internal states that cannot be observed.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a needs analysis before building a course?

options.label: To choose the slide template and the delivery platform for the course content
To find the gap between current and desired performance and whether training can close it
To write the final exam questions and set the passing score before any content has been developed
To gather learner opinions on how enjoyable earlier courses were and which formats they liked best

rubric: Needs analysis defines the performance gap and its causes, including non-training causes.
Distractors confuse analysis with development tasks or with satisfaction feedback.

items.prompt: A trainer gives a short ungraded quiz halfway through a workshop and changes the second half based on the results. How is this quiz best classified?

options.label: Reaction evaluation, because it asks how learners feel about the session
Formative assessment, because the results are used to adjust teaching in progress
Summative assessment, because it measures learning at a fixed point in time
Needs analysis, because it collects information about the learners

rubric: Formative assessment informs ongoing instruction and is low stakes.
Summative is tempting because it is a measurement, but it is not used for final judgement.

items.prompt: Why should objectives, learning activities and assessments be aligned with each other?

options.label: So that learners practise and are tested on the skills the course set out to teach
So that the course can be delivered in less time because activities and assessments overlap
So that learners are certain to pass the assessment on their first attempt after the activities
So that the course looks consistent, with every module following the same layout and format

rubric: Alignment means practice and testing match the intended outcomes.
Distractors confuse alignment with visual consistency, guaranteed passing or speed.

items.prompt: Why do designers often split a complex procedure into short chunks with practice after each one?

options.label: Because learners prefer shorter sessions, and higher satisfaction ratings lead to better results
Because working memory is limited, so smaller pieces are easier to process and retain
Because practice after each chunk replaces the need for any final assessment of learners
Because learners absorb content best when each chunk is passively reviewed before any practice

rubric: Chunking manages cognitive load because working memory holds little at once.
Distractors rest on preference or on false claims about assessment and accuracy.

items.prompt: Which are benefits of writing clear learning objectives? Select all that apply.

options.label: They remove the need to evaluate the course afterwards
They guide the choice of suitable assessments
They tell learners what to focus their effort on
They guarantee that learners will use the skill on the job

rubric: Clear objectives direct assessment design and learner focus.
No objective guarantees transfer or replaces evaluation.

items.prompt: After a safety course, a company sends learners a form asking how useful and enjoyable they found it. A manager says this shows whether workers learned the safety rules. Using Kirkpatrick's four levels, what does the form actually measure?

options.label: Level 3 behaviour, since it shows what workers do on the floor
Level 4 results, since it shows the effect on company safety figures
Level 2 learning, since it shows what knowledge was gained
Level 1 reaction, since it captures learners' opinions of the course

rubric: Satisfaction forms measure reaction, level 1.
Learners' opinions do not show knowledge, behaviour change or business results.

items.prompt: A designer needs an objective for a module on handling pricing objections. Which objective best includes performance, condition and standard?

options.label: After the workshop, reps will feel confident responding whenever customers question the price of the product
Given a recorded customer objection, reps will respond using the three-step model with no missed steps
Reps will understand the three-step model for pricing objections and why each step matters to customers
During role-play, reps will be exposed to the common pricing objections raised by customers in the past year

rubric: It states the condition, the observable performance and the standard.
Distractors are vague, describe exposure, or describe a feeling.

items.prompt: You are teaching beginners to build pivot tables in a spreadsheet. Which sequence is best?

options.label: Show a finished dashboard first, then take it apart one part at a time in the order they appear
Show data layout rules, build a simple pivot table, then add filters and calculated fields
Teach each menu option in depth one at a time, then have learners build a table at the end
Start with calculated fields, then explain data layout, then build the first table

rubric: Simple-to-complex sequencing builds on prior steps for beginners.
Other sequences begin with advanced content or have no logical build-up.

items.prompt: The objective is: 'Nurses will perform chest compressions at the correct depth and rate.' Which activity fits best?

options.label: Reading a detailed article on the physiology of cardiac arrest
Completing a multiple-choice quiz on compression guidelines
Watching an expert's lecture on compression technique
Practising on a feedback manikin that shows depth and rate

rubric: Skill objectives need hands-on practice with feedback.
The other activities build knowledge about compressions but do not practise the skill.

items.prompt: The objective is: 'Supervisors will calculate overtime pay for a given shift.' Which assessment best matches it?

options.label: Ask them to name the law that sets overtime rules in a multiple-choice item
Ask them to define overtime in their own words in a short answer
Ask them to rate their confidence in overtime rules on a scale
Give three sample shift records and ask them to compute the overtime pay

rubric: The assessment has to require the same calculation that the objective names.
The distractors test definitions, confidence or recall instead of calculation.

items.prompt: A designer interviews supervisors and reviews error logs to learn why order mistakes happen. Which ADDIE phase is this?

options.label: Evaluation
Design
Implementation
Analysis

rubric: Collecting data on performance problems and causes is analysis.
Design plans objectives and strategy; evaluation judges results after delivery.

items.prompt: The objective is 'Give constructive feedback to a colleague.' Which activities give learners practice with feedback? Select all that apply.

options.label: Watch a lecture on the history of performance reviews
Role-play a feedback conversation while an observer uses a checklist
Practise scripted scenarios in pairs and get peer comments
Read a long article about feedback theory

rubric: Both involve doing the skill and getting feedback on it.
Reading and lecture build knowledge but give no practice.

items.prompt: A 30-minute e-learning module introduces 12 new terms and a six-step procedure in one stretch. Pilot learners say they feel overwhelmed and cannot complete the procedure afterwards. Which redesign best applies cognitive load principles?

options.label: Add a background history of the procedure up front so learners have fuller context before they meet the new terms and steps
Remove the practice activities so learners have more of the 30 minutes to read and absorb all of the terms and steps
Split it into short segments, teaching a few terms and steps and adding practice after each
Add more on-screen text so every term is explained in greater detail and learners need not rely on memory

rubric: Segmenting with practice reduces load and builds the procedure gradually.
The distractors add load or remove practice, worsening the problem.

items.prompt: You are writing a measurable objective for a safety course. Which version best meets the standard of an observable, measurable objective?

options.label: By the end of the course, the learner will fully understand how to handle chemical spills safely and correctly
The learner will appreciate why spill cleanup rules exist and value following them in every workplace situation
The learner will be aware of the importance of spill response procedures and of the risks of ignoring them
Given a spill scenario, the learner will select the correct cleanup procedure with no errors

rubric: It names a condition, an observable action and a criterion.
Understand, be aware and appreciate are unobservable verbs, so they cannot be assessed directly.

items.prompt: A course teaches a 5-step invoicing procedure to new clerks. Using a task-analysis approach, which sequence of instruction best fits a procedure that must be done in order?

options.label: Teach the steps in the order performed, practising each step before a full run-through
Teach the steps grouped by difficulty, easiest first, then run the whole procedure once at the end
Teach the final step first and work backward, since the finished invoice is what clerks are judged on
Teach the hardest step first so that later steps feel easier by comparison, then add the rest

rubric: Procedural tasks are best sequenced in performance order with practice.
Hardest-first ignores the dependency of steps on each other.

items.prompt: You must check whether learners can troubleshoot a printer fault, a performance skill. Which assessment item matches the objective most directly?

options.label: A multiple-choice quiz on printer parts, their functions and common error codes
A written exam asking learners to list the steps for clearing a paper jam
A short essay explaining how printer faults arise and how technicians fix them
A simulation where the learner diagnoses and fixes a printer fault

rubric: Assessment should match the performance in the objective.
Recall and essay formats test knowledge about printers, not the skill of fixing them.

items.prompt: A needs analysis shows learners already know the theory of customer greeting but fail to use it on calls because they feel nervous. Which activity should you add?

options.label: A longer lecture on greeting theory with extra slides and definitions
Role-play practice calls with feedback and gradually rising difficulty
A reading list of books on communication history and linguistics
A glossary of greeting terms to memorise before the next session

rubric: The gap is performance confidence, so rehearsal with feedback fits.
More theory addresses a knowledge gap that does not exist.

items.prompt: You apply Kirkpatrick's four levels to a sales training programme. Which measure belongs at Level 3 (Behavior)?

options.label: Learner ratings of the trainer, the room and the materials collected on the final day
Change in company revenue per sales region during the year following the training
Manager observation of reps using the new questioning technique on live calls
Scores on an end-of-day knowledge quiz about the new questioning technique and its steps

rubric: Level 3 measures on-the-job behaviour change after training.
Ratings are Level 1, quizzes Level 2, and business revenue is Level 4.

items.prompt: You are drafting a learning objective using the ABCD model (Audience, Behavior, Condition, Degree). Which parts below are correctly applied elements of that model? Select all that apply.

options.label: Degree: with at least 90 percent accuracy within 10 minutes
Behavior: will be more motivated to write clearly
Condition: using the company style guide and no spell-checker
Audience: a four-hour workshop on clinical documentation for the pediatric ward

items.prompt: You are building a 2-hour module on using a new expense app. The objective is: employees will submit a correct expense claim in the app. You have a short lecture, a sandbox version of the app and a quiz tool. Which design applies the objective best?

options.label: Demonstrate once, then have learners submit practice claims in the sandbox with feedback
Give a handout on expense policy history and ask learners to summarise the key rules
Let learners explore the live app alone and email questions afterwards
Deliver a 90-minute lecture on every menu in the app, then run a 10-question recall quiz

rubric: Practising the target task in a safe environment matches the objective.
A lecture plus quiz tests recall, not submitting claims; unguided live use risks errors.

items.prompt: After a compliance course, 95 percent of learners pass the quiz, yet audits show the same errors on the job. Which diagnosis is most plausible?

options.label: Learners lack interest in compliance, so the quiz results reflect guessing rather than learning
The quiz tests recall while the job needs applied judgement, so the two are misaligned
The course covered too little content, so learners could pass only by memorising the quiz items
The pass mark was set too low, so most learners passed without mastering the content

rubric: High passes with job errors point to misalignment between assessment and performance.
Difficulty and length do not explain high pass rates.

items.prompt: A needs analysis finds that technicians make errors because the reference manual is out of date and unclear. Which analysis of the situation is soundest?

options.label: It is a motivation problem, so incentives should replace all instruction
It is a hiring problem, so the programme should screen out weak technicians
It is partly a performance-support problem, so training alone will not fix it
It is purely a knowledge gap, so a longer course is the correct fix

rubric: Environmental causes such as faulty job aids cannot be solved by training alone.
The other options assign cause to knowledge, motivation or hiring without evidence.

items.prompt: A module on statistics puts hypothesis testing before the concepts of mean and variance, and learners struggle. What is the best analysis of the cause?

options.label: The module had too many images, which distracted learners from reading
Prerequisite concepts were sequenced after the skills that depend on them
Learners were given too much feedback during the first activity
Hypothesis testing is inherently unteachable in short modules

rubric: Skills depending on prior concepts need those concepts taught first.
The other causes are not supported by the described sequencing.

items.prompt: Two versions of a course teach the same objective. Version A has learners passively watch videos; version B has them solve cases with feedback. B shows higher transfer on the job. Which comparison best explains why?

options.label: B exposes learners to more content and examples, and greater coverage of material tends to raise transfer
B is more engaging and motivating, and higher learner enjoyment tends to carry over into later job performance
B has learners retrieve and apply knowledge in job-like contexts and get corrective feedback
B takes less seat time, and shorter courses tend to reduce overload and so improve application on the job

rubric: Practice with feedback in similar contexts supports transfer.
Entertainment, volume and brevity do not by themselves explain transfer.

items.prompt: A pilot shows that learners with prior experience finish a module quickly and report boredom, while novices fail the final task. What does this pattern most directly suggest about the design?

options.label: It ignores differing prior knowledge; add pre-assessment or branching paths
The module is too short overall; lengthen it with more content for every learner
The final task is too hard for the course level; replace it with an easier one
Experienced learners lack motivation; add badges and rewards to keep them engaged

rubric: Mixed expertise calls for pre-assessment or differentiated paths.
Uniform changes leave one group poorly served.

items.prompt: A course's post-test scores are high, but a learner survey shows low confidence and managers report no behavior change. Which findings would help locate the cause? Select all that apply.

options.label: Whether workplace systems or managers support using the new skills
Whether learners rated the course facilitator as friendly and engaging
Whether learners had chances to practise with feedback before the test
Whether test items mirror the on-the-job tasks in the objectives

rubric: Alignment, practice and workplace support each affect transfer.
Carpet colour has no plausible link to behavior change.

items.prompt: A call-centre course aims to cut average handling time. Post-course, learners know the new scripts, but handling time is unchanged. Observation shows the CRM system takes 40 seconds to load each screen. What is the best analysis?

options.label: Learners lack motivation to apply the scripts, so the course should add a motivation session on the value of speed
The assessment did not measure real performance, so it should be redesigned around timed live-call simulations
The scripts were too short to cover calls, so adding more scripts will cut handling time
A system delay outside training limits handling time, so content redesign alone won't meet the goal

rubric: Evidence shows a systemic barrier, not a knowledge gap.
Other options ignore the observed cause.

items.prompt: A safety course shows 95% completion and an average post-test score of 92%, yet audits find no change in how workers perform the inspection. Which diagnosis best fits this pattern?

options.label: The course was too short, so workers could not retain enough to change their behavior.
The completion data was inaccurate because the LMS recorded views instead of true attendance.
The post-test measured recall of course content, not the inspection performance the course targeted.
Workers lacked motivation, so they skimmed the content and then guessed on the test.

rubric: High scores with no performance change point to assessment and objectives that were not aligned to the job task.
Motivation, tracking and length explanations ignore that learners did demonstrably pass the test.

items.prompt: After a sales workshop, reps score well on a role-play but rarely use the new discovery technique with customers. Interviews show commissions reward fast closes, and discovery calls take longer. What does this finding indicate?

options.label: The barrier is environmental: more training won't help unless the incentives change.
The practice activities lacked spaced repetition, so the skill decayed within a few weeks.
The facilitators modelled the technique poorly, so reps copied a weaker version of the method.
The role-play was too easy, so it overstated how well reps had actually learned the technique.

rubric: Reps can perform the skill but are penalised for using it, which is a non-training cause.
Other options assume a learning deficit, but the evidence shows the skill was learned.

items.prompt: Post-course surveys show learners rated a workshop 4.7/5 for enjoyment, yet scores on a scenario-based test were low. Which analysis is most defensible?

options.label: The survey sample was probably biased toward happy learners, so the satisfaction data should be set aside and the course redesigned.
The facilitator's charisma likely inflated the ratings, which suggests the content itself was weak and needs rewriting.
The test was probably too hard, because scenario items demand more than the content learners studied and practised.
Enjoyment did not translate into practice on the tested skill, so activities likely did not match the objective.

rubric: Reaction and learning measure different things; low learning with high reaction suggests activities not aligned to the objective.
The other options make unsupported leaps about bias, unfairness or facilitator effects.

items.prompt: A pretest for a spreadsheet course shows two clusters: half the audience scored near zero and half near ceiling. The single linear course gets poor feedback from both groups. What best explains the pattern?

options.label: Novices lack motivation to start without engaging hooks, while experts resist the course because completion requirements feel too lenient.
Both groups dislike self-paced formats, since learners at either extreme need a live instructor to keep their attention and pace.
Novices are overloaded by unscaffolded steps while experts are slowed by guidance they no longer need.
The pretest was invalid, because a split into two clusters like this usually points to poorly written or ambiguous items.

rubric: This is the expertise reversal effect: one path suits neither extreme.
The other options attribute the problem to format, item validity or motivation without evidence.

items.prompt: An e-learning module shows dense diagrams while a narrator reads aloud the same text printed on screen. Learners do poorly on transfer questions. Which element most likely causes the problem?

options.label: The narration pace is slower than reading speed, so learners lose attention and encode the material weakly.
The diagrams carry too much detail for novices, and removing them would raise transfer scores.
The transfer questions test far beyond the module content, so the learners' results say little about the design.
Narration duplicating the on-screen text adds redundant processing and extraneous cognitive load.

rubric: Duplicating narration with on-screen text creates redundancy and extra load that can reduce transfer.
Removing visuals or blaming speed or questions misses the specific redundancy mechanism.

items.prompt: A pilot shows post-test scores rose 40 points, yet supervisors see no improvement in the trained task. Which are plausible causes that an analysis of the course should check? Select all that apply.

options.label: Test items reuse wording from the slides, so learners can answer by recognition rather than by performing.
The test measures knowledge objectives while the job task requires applying a procedure under time pressure.
The pilot group was larger than the planned rollout group, which invalidates all score gains.
The pilot ran for more days than the rollout, which means supervisors cannot see any change.
Scores rose because learners saw the exact test items in a pretest and practiced them during the course.

rubric: Recognition cues, a mismatch between test and task, and test-item exposure can all inflate scores without job transfer.
Group size and pilot duration do not explain the gap between test scores and job performance.

items.prompt: A hospital's mandatory medication-safety course shows 98% completion, yet error rates are unchanged. Interviews reveal nurses click through quickly. The quiz allows unlimited retakes with the correct answer shown after each miss. Which design feature most directly explains why quiz scores do not predict practice?

options.label: Completion tracking counts page clicks rather than time on task, so the 98% figure is meaningless.
Learners can pass by trial and error, so scores do not reflect skill.
Because the course is mandatory, learners cannot develop intrinsic interest, so they disengage from the content.
The quiz has too few items to give a reliable score for each nurse, so individual results vary by chance.

rubric: Retakes with answers revealed allow guess-and-check passing, so scores no longer indicate mastery.
Mandatory status, item count and tracking do not explain why passing fails to predict practice.

items.prompt: A firm will train 200 staff in waves over six months. Leaders want credible evidence that training, not other factors, improved a customer-complaint metric, at low cost. Which evaluation plan best meets these criteria?

options.label: Survey every participant after each wave and report average satisfaction and self-rated confidence as evidence that the training changed their behaviour.
Compare complaint rates for trained waves against not-yet-trained waves, using the staggered rollout as a comparison.
Give every participant an end-of-course test and compare the average score to the passing threshold to show the skills were learned.
Ask managers at six months whether they believe the training improved complaints, and report the share who say that it did.

rubric: Staggered waves give a low-cost comparison group on the actual business metric, supporting attribution.
Satisfaction, test scores and opinions do not isolate training's effect on complaints.

items.prompt: Novices must learn a 12-step billing procedure. Criteria: fast learning, low error rates in the first month, and a modest development budget. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: A reading-based manual followed by a final multiple-choice test on step order.
A high-fidelity simulation from the first session, so learners meet realistic complexity at once.
A discovery-based task where learners work out the procedure from system errors.
Worked examples that fade into partially completed practice, then full practice on realistic cases.

rubric: Novices learn procedures efficiently from worked examples with faded support, at modest cost.
Early simulation and discovery overload novices, and a manual with a test does not build performance.

items.prompt: Criteria for an objective: observable, tied to the real job task, and stating conditions and a standard. Which objective best meets all three for a help-desk course?

options.label: By the end of the course, learners will understand the ticketing system and all 15 of its categories well enough to support customers.
Learners will appreciate the importance of accurate ticket categorisation in customer service.
Learners will know the 15 ticket categories and be familiar with escalation guidance.
Given 10 live-style tickets, learners will categorise at least 9 correctly without a reference guide.

rubric: It names an observable action, conditions (10 tickets, no guide) and a standard (9 correct) on a real task.
The others use unobservable verbs such as appreciate, understand, know and be familiar with.

items.prompt: A plan says training succeeded if the average reaction score is at least 4.5/5. The goal is for supervisors to give effective feedback on the floor. Which revision best fixes the plan?

options.label: Raise the threshold to 4.8 so that only exceptional programs count as successful.
Add a checklist for observing feedback on the floor after training, alongside the reaction survey.
Keep the reaction score and add a question asking whether learners plan to give feedback.
Replace the survey with a longer one, since more questions will give a more reliable reaction score.

rubric: The goal is behavior, so evidence must come from observed on-the-job performance.
A higher threshold, a longer survey or an intent question still only measures reactions or intentions.

items.prompt: A distributed team of 60 must learn a negotiation skill. Criteria: accessible across time zones, includes feedback on actual performance, and limited facilitator hours. Which design best fits?

options.label: Short self-paced lessons on concepts, plus small live practice sessions where a facilitator coaches role-plays.
Short self-paced lessons on concepts, plus a discussion forum where peers post comments on each other's negotiation write-ups.
Fully self-paced video lectures by an expert negotiator, with an auto-graded scenario quiz and instant scores at the end.
One long live lecture each quarter by a senior negotiator, recorded for people who cannot attend, with slides shared.

rubric: Self-paced concepts save facilitator time and fit time zones, while small coached practice supplies performance feedback.
Video with a quiz, lectures and forums offer little feedback on actual performance.

items.prompt: A stakeholder wants two more hours of content added to a course that already meets its objectives. Which are sound reasons to push back, judged against learning goals and constraints? Select all that apply.

options.label: A job aid or follow-up resource may cover the extra material without lengthening the course.
Stakeholders should not influence content, since only instructional designers can decide what belongs.
Content unlinked to an objective adds load and dilutes the practice time that drives performance.
Longer courses always score lower on satisfaction, so any added time will lower ratings.
Added content should be tested against the needs analysis; if it addresses no performance gap, it is not justified.

rubric: Sound pushback ties content to objectives, performance gaps and alternatives like job aids.
Blanket claims about satisfaction or excluding stakeholders are not defensible criteria.

items.prompt: A team has two weeks to support a tax-adjustment procedure that staff perform about twice a year. It has 30 steps with exact rates, and errors are costly. They can build a full course or a job aid with a short practice exercise. Judging by frequency, error cost and time, which choice is best?

options.label: Skip support entirely, since staff will learn the procedure by doing it twice a year.
Build the full course, because high error costs always call for comprehensive training.
Build an open-ended discovery activity, so learners derive the rates themselves and remember them.
Build a job aid with a short practice exercise, since rare, detail-heavy tasks suit reference support.

rubric: Rare, detail-heavy tasks are poorly retained, so a job aid plus brief practice fits the time and the risk.
A full course will decay before use, skipping support ignores cost, and discovery of exact rates is unreliable.

items.prompt: A team says its new course caused a 20% drop in order-entry errors, because errors fell in the quarter after rollout. No comparison group or pre-rollout trend data exist. Which critique of this claim is strongest?

options.label: Error rates are a results-level measure, and results can never be tied to training under any evaluation design, even a controlled one.
Satisfaction scores should replace error data, because they show directly that the course changed learner behaviour on the job.
A 20% drop is too small to count, since training impact is only credible when it exceeds a 50% threshold of improvement.
With no baseline, the drop may reflect seasonality, staffing changes or a software release rather than the course.

rubric: Attribution needs a baseline or comparison to rule out rival explanations.
Distractors wrongly claim results are unattributable, prefer reaction data, or invent a fixed threshold.

items.prompt: One course must serve both true novices and experienced practitioners, and the platform has no adaptive engine. Criteria: avoid wasting expert time, avoid overloading novices, and keep one build. Which design decision is the best trade-off?

options.label: Remove most guidance so everyone solves open problems first, since discovery builds deeper understanding than worked examples for novices.
Pitch all content at the average learner's level, since a single middle path serves both groups with the least build effort.
Use a short pretest to route experienced learners to problem-solving tasks and novices to worked examples with fading support.
Give everyone the same fully worked examples, since extra guidance helps experienced learners confirm their knowledge and costs little time.

rubric: Guidance helps novices but can hinder experts (expertise reversal), so routing by prior knowledge fits the criteria.
Distractors ignore that the same support has different effects on different learners.

items.prompt: Sales reps can correctly describe the quoting process in interviews, yet they skip it. Analysis shows the bonus plan rewards speed of closing and penalises delays. A manager asks for a refresher course. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Add a certification test on the quoting process, because a real consequence for failing will make reps follow every step in practice.
Fix the conflicting incentive first, because training cannot close a gap caused by the environment rather than missing skill.
Build a motivational module on the value of quoting, since reps skip steps when they do not appreciate why each step matters.
Build the refresher, because any gap between knowing and doing is best closed by repeating the process with more supervised practice.

rubric: The cause is an environmental barrier, so training is the wrong main intervention.
Distractors treat a performance-environment problem as a knowledge or attitude problem.

items.prompt: A course objective says learners will 'diagnose faults in a conveyor control system'. The final assessment is a 40-item multiple-choice test of component names and definitions. What is the most serious weakness of this assessment?

options.label: It is too short, because any valid assessment needs at least 100 items to give a defensible result.
It is norm-referenced by nature, so scores only rank learners and cannot show whether anyone met the objective.
It is unreliable because multiple-choice scoring is subjective, so different graders would give different marks.
It measures recall of terms rather than diagnostic performance, so passing is weak evidence the objective was met.

rubric: Validity depends on alignment between objective and assessed performance.
Distractors misstate MCQ scoring, length rules and norm-referencing.

items.prompt: Budget covers only one format for training staff on an emergency shutdown. The event is rare, performed under stress, and errors are costly. Criteria: fidelity to real conditions, practice with feedback, and transfer. Which option is best?

options.label: A scenario simulation with coached feedback, because matched conditions support transfer.
A signed attestation of having read the procedure, because it creates accountability and a documented record that staff know each step.
A recorded expert lecture on the procedure, because it reaches staff at the lowest cost and is easy to update when steps change.
A self-paced module with a scored quiz, because retention scores can be tracked and reported for each learner.

rubric: Rare, stressful, high-cost tasks need realistic practice with feedback.
Distractors favour cost, reporting or accountability over transfer.

items.prompt: A leadership program is evaluated only by an end-of-course satisfaction survey and a knowledge test. The program goal is better team performance. Which are valid criticisms of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Satisfaction surveys are invalid and must be dropped, because learner reactions have no link to learning conditions.
Knowledge tests should never be used in program evaluation, since they cannot inform any decision.
It does not connect any measure to the team-performance goal the program was funded to achieve.
It gives no evidence that managers changed behaviour on the job after the course.
It lacks a baseline and delayed follow-up, so lasting change cannot be separated from short-term recall.

rubric: The plan stops at reaction and learning, missing behaviour, durability and results.
Options 4 and 5 overstate: knowledge tests and reaction data have limited but real uses.

items.prompt: Field technicians may leave the job for at most two days per quarter. The design lead must choose a format for a skill that must still be retained at 90 days. Options: a two-day workshop alone, six weekly half-day sessions, or a workshop plus later spaced prompts. Which judgement best fits the constraint and the retention goal?

options.label: Run the two-day workshop alone, since the time limit decides the matter and retention can be assumed after hands-on work.
Extend the workshop to five days, because longer contact time produces more durable learning than spacing does.
Run six weekly half-day sessions, since spacing is the strongest retention factor and justifies exceeding the limit.
Run the two-day workshop, then send short mobile retrieval tasks over following weeks to fit time limits and support retention.

rubric: The hybrid respects the release-time limit and adds spaced retrieval for durability.
Distractors ignore either the constraint or the retention criterion.

items.prompt: Design an assessment for 'negotiate a contract renewal'. Constraints: 200 learners, only four available raters, and results must be reliable and reflect actual performance. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: A 50-item multiple-choice test on negotiation terms and tactics, auto-scored and item-analysed for all 200 learners.
Role-plays scored with an anchored rubric, after raters calibrate on sample recordings and double-score a sample.
Peer-scored role-plays in pairs, where each partner rates the other with a short checklist and no rater training.
Learner self-ratings of confidence after the course, collected through a short online survey with set scale anchors.

rubric: A rubric with calibration and sampled double-scoring gives reliable performance evidence with few raters.
Distractors fail on performance validity or reliability.

items.prompt: Design a sequence for teaching incident triage to learners with no prior knowledge. Constraints: the task is complex, the components interact, and learners must integrate them in real work. Which plan fits?

options.label: Order lessons by the chapter structure of the reference manual, ending with practice on realistic cases.
Open with the hardest real incident to motivate learners, then backfill any needed knowledge afterwards.
Use whole tasks from simple to complex, with support that fades as each task class is mastered.
Teach each component in isolation, then integrate everything in a single final capstone case.

rubric: Whole-task sequencing with fading support suits interacting components and integration needs.
Distractors delay integration, follow content structure, or overload novices.

items.prompt: A self-paced course loses 40% of learners at module 3, where a quiz needs a skill never taught. Constraints: total seat time cannot grow, and objectives must stay unchanged. Which fix meets both?

options.label: Remove the module 3 quiz entirely, since removing the barrier is the quickest way to keep learners moving.
Add a short diagnostic that branches only those who need it into a brief refresher, leaving the main path unchanged.
Lower the module 3 passing score so that fewer learners are blocked and the dropout rate falls.
Add badges and a leaderboard to module 3, since the stall reflects low motivation rather than missing skill.

rubric: The data point to a missing prerequisite; branching adds it only for those who need it.
Distractors lower standards, misdiagnose motivation or remove the assessment.

items.prompt: Expert technicians perform a diagnostic task well but cannot list their steps when asked. You must build content that captures their real decision-making. Which design for the analysis phase fits?

options.label: Run critical-incident interviews on past hard cases and observe live work to elicit tacit decision rules.
Copy the existing equipment manual into the course, since its documented procedures already capture what experts do.
Ask each expert to write the step list from memory, then have a peer edit it for clarity into a job aid.
Survey all technicians about which steps they consider most important, then rank the results by average rating.

rubric: Cognitive task analysis methods surface tacit knowledge that experts cannot easily articulate.
Distractors rely on self-reported steps or documents that miss tacit decisions.

items.prompt: Design a transfer support for a negotiation course. Constraints: managers can give at most 15 minutes in total per learner, and the support must prompt real on-the-job use within 30 days. Which design meets them?

options.label: A weekly one-hour coaching meeting between each learner and their manager for the three months after the course, focused on real negotiations.
A second full-day workshop at 30 days that repeats the key content with new role-plays, since spaced repetition drives application.
A 10-minute pre-course manager brief, a real-work application task, and a 30-day prompt with a short check-in.
An end-of-course certificate plus an automated email series with negotiation tips sent weekly, leaving managers out entirely.

rubric: The design fits the manager time limit while linking learning to real work with a timed prompt.
Distractors exceed the time limit or lack on-the-job application.

items.prompt: A draft course on lockout/tagout has the objective 'perform the lockout sequence correctly', a video lecture, and a knowledge quiz. Constraints: learners must practise the actual performance, get feedback, and be assessed validly. Which additions meet them? Select all that apply.

options.label: Feedback to learners against a step-by-step checklist during practice.
Hands-on or simulated practice of the full lockout sequence on representative equipment.
A points leaderboard showing quiz scores across all learners in the cohort.
Extra video chapters on the regulatory history of workplace safety law.
An observed performance assessment scored with the same checklist.

rubric: Practice, feedback and performance assessment align the course with the performance objective.
History content and leaderboards add neither practice nor valid assessment.

items.prompt: A designer must show that a new onboarding program shortens time-to-productivity. Constraints: random assignment is not allowed, cohorts start monthly, and HR holds ramp-up data for past cohorts. Which evaluation design meets all constraints?

options.label: Compare the new cohort with prior cohorts' ramp data, stagger rollout across teams, and track hiring-mix variables.
Randomly assign new hires to old or new onboarding, so differences can be attributed to the program alone.
Survey managers after the first month on whether the new hires seem to be ramping up faster.
Compare end-of-program quiz scores with the previous cohort's scores as the main evidence of faster ramp-up.

rubric: Historical baselines plus staggered rollout give credible quasi-experimental evidence without randomisation.
Distractors violate the no-random-assignment constraint or use weak proxies.
